text: Ever wondered how sugar gets into a cell, when the membrane is built to keep water-loving things out? Your cells trade with their surroundings all the time. In your lungs, oxygen moves into red blood cells. Glucose dissolved in your blood plasma reaches cells that use it in respiration. Water moves into and out of cells constantly. Yet a cell surface membrane has a hydrophobic core, and glucose, a polar molecule, does not cross that core readily. So how does it get in? And how much of this traffic costs the cell any energy at all?
